query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Post-deposition annealing that creates a bimodal grain size distribution in FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings stabilizes nanoscale grain boundaries during high‐temperature sliding by promoting controlled dynamic recrystallization and continuous protective oxide film formation, leading to reduced wear compared to as-deposited nanocrystalline coatings.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited nanocrystalline FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating on a conventional metal substrate.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled post-deposition annealing treatment designed to induce a bimodal grain size distribution in the coating.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests conducted at elevated temperatures (500–700°C) under loads representative of real high-temperature environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale grain boundaries and their evolution during dynamic recrystallization.
generation.mechanism: The annealing-induced bimodal grain structure stabilizes critical grain boundaries during high-temperature sliding, which in turn promotes a controlled dynamic recrystallization process that facilitates the formation of a uniform and continuous protective oxide layer, ultimately reducing the coating’s material loss.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under high-temperature sliding conditions, the annealed (bimodal-grained) coating will exhibit a significantly lower wear rate and the presence of a continuous protective oxide film, while the as-deposited nanocrystalline coating will show higher wear and less uniform oxide formation.
generation.baseline: The as-deposited nanocrystalline FeNiCrCoCu coating without any annealing treatment.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to thin-film protective coatings on conventional metal substrates under high-temperature sliding wear conditions (500–700°C). Variations in substrate type or significantly different thermal/mechanical regimes may alter the operative mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: Although prior studies and trends in high-entropy alloy coatings support the role of grain boundary stabilization in enhancing oxide film formation, the exact balance between improved protective oxide development and potential grain boundary weakening at extreme conditions remains uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu coatings: one set in the as-deposited nanocrystalline state and another set subjected to controlled annealing to develop a bimodal grain size distribution. Subject both sets to identical sliding wear tests at 500–700°C under representative high-temperature loads.
measurements: Wear rate assessment via mass loss measurements
Microstructural characterization using SEM, EBSD, and TEM to evaluate grain structure and dynamic recrystallization features
Surface composition analysis (XRD, EDS) to assess the continuity and composition of the oxide layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed coatings do not show a statistically significant reduction in wear rate or fail to develop a continuous, protective oxide film compared to the as-deposited coatings under the specified high-temperature sliding conditions, the hypothesis will be falsified.

In equimolar HEAs, each element has an equal probability of occupying the lattice sites in a crystal structure such as face-centered cubic (FCC), [2] body-centered cubic (BCC), [3] or hexagonal structure [4] crystal structures. Abstract In this paper, the Si-20Cr-20Fe coating was prepared on MoNbTaTiW RHEA by a fused slurry method. The microstructural evolution and compositions of the silicide coating under high-temperature oxidation environment were studied. The results show that the silicide coating could effectively prevent the oxidation of the MoNbTaTiW RHEA. The initial silicide coating had a double-layer structure: a high silicon content layer mainly composed of MSi 2 as the outer layer and a low silicon content layer mainly contained M 5 Si 3 as the inner layer. Under high-temperature oxidation conditions, the silicon element diffused from the silicide coating to the RHEA substrate while the oxidation of the coating occurred. After oxidation, the coating was composed of an outer oxide layer and an inner silicide layer. The silicide layer moved toward the inside of the substrate, led to the increase of its thickness. Compared with the initial silicified layer, its structure did not change significantly. The structure and compositions of the oxide layer on the outer surface strongly depended on the oxidation temperature. frame.understanding: The hypothesis is that the overall wear resistance of the FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating at high temperatures is governed by the stability and evolution of nanoscale grain boundaries, which in turn regulate dynamic recrystallization and the formation of a continuous, protective oxide film during wear. As the temperature increases, the nanocrystalline structure can transform via thermally activated processes that either strengthen the coating through refined oxide-layer formation or weaken it if grain boundary sliding and interfacial degradation dominate. An optimal grain size distribution (e.g., a bimodal structure achieved via controlled annealing) may promote stable oxide formation and reduced material loss under load.

decision.trend: Earlier efforts on high-entropy alloy coatings began with altering composition, grain size, and coating–substrate combinations and focused mainly on room‐temperature wear. Subsequent work, such as that on the AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 system, extended testing into high-temperature regimes and highlighted that wear improvements at elevated temperatures can be linked to microstructural evolution—specifically, dynamic grain boundary activity that promotes the formation of continuous, protective oxide films. However, these studies largely treated the alloy in isolation or within a narrow thermal window, leaving the integrated coating–substrate response under broad high-temperature conditions insufficiently explored.
decision.unsolved: It remains unclear how the evolution of nanoscale grain boundaries in the as-deposited nanocrystalline FeNiCrCoCu coating governs dynamic recrystallization and subsequent protective oxide film formation during sliding wear at high temperatures. In particular, the potential benefits of achieving an optimal (e.g., bimodal) grain size distribution for stabilizing these processes across the coating–substrate interface have not been demonstrated.
decision.lever: Implement post-deposition annealing to induce a bimodal grain size distribution in the FeNiCrCoCu coating
decision.why: This approach directly builds on the trend observed in earlier studies: tuning grain boundary stability can promote controlled dynamic recrystallization and uniform oxide film development. By moving from the as-deposited nanocrystalline state to a deliberately engineered bimodal structure, the experiment can test whether such microstructural optimization improves wear resistance under high-temperature sliding (e.g., 500–700°C) compared to the baseline. The expected observation is that the annealed coating will form a continuous, protective oxide layer with reduced material loss, whereas a failure to observe improved wear would falsify the mechanistic hypothesis.
